newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi hits back at talk of crisis.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi hits back at talk of crisis.

text.p: Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi brushed off talk that his tenure was at risk as a national obsession on Tuesday after headline writers seized on opposition predictions that his government was destined to collapse.

Prodi, leader since May of a centre-left cabinet he has said will last an unprecedented five years, hit back from a European security summit in Lisbon after yet more speculation that a crisis in his "Olive Tree" coalition was waiting to happen.
"It is hard for people to get used to a government lasting the life of a parliament after 50 years in which we've had 54 governments," Prodi said.
"What's really needed is a psychological change and that takes time," he told Italian television.

Prodi led his alliance to a narrow victory last April in a general election widely seen as a further step in the slow political transition Italy has been undergoing since devastating graft scandals brought down its old governing class in 1992.
Centre-right opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi, prime minister for just seven months in 1994, forecast on Monday night that Prodi's government would fall apart next spring.

He said the crisis would come over a supplementary budget many economic analysts believe the government will have to draw up to ensure its 1997 accounts meet the conditions for Italian membership of a planned European single currency.
He coupled his prediction with an unexpected offer to bring his Freedom Alliance into a broad-based government to work on economic and constitutional reform if Prodi were to fall.
The offer, at odds with Berlusconi's past insistence on elections as the only solution when a government collapses, was rejected out of hand by Prodi.
"The age of these grand coalitions without a programme is over," Prodi said.

Italy has been governed for much of the past four years of political upheaval by technocrat cabinets led by Carlo Azeglio Ciampi and Lamberto Dini, now respectively treasury minister and foreign minister in Prodi's government.

The April election was seen as a watershed in a gradually emerging new landscape of two competing political blocs formed from the plethora of parties which are vying for the space left by the collapse of the old guard.

All parties agree that further change is vital but deep differences have so far prevented moves to begin work on reforming the constitution, refining the electoral system and re-defining the powers of government and parliament.

Prodi's coalition is far from homogenous, ranging from Dini's centrist Italian Renewal Party to the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left and dependent for its survival on external support from the hardline Communist Refoundation party.

Strains have been apparent on several occasions, notably on economic policy and the structure of a 62.5 trillion lire ($40 billion) deficit-cutting budget the government has drawn up to try to squeeze in to Europe's planned monetary union.
Dini has called repeatedly for the coalition to look to centrists in Berlusconi's bloc for reinforcement, a formula that has raised hackles in Communist Refoundation.

In a sign of the tensions, Dini accused the government in published remarks on Monday of failing to consult Italian Renewal on policy and warned that the party would pull out of the coalition if there were "another discourtesy of this sort".
